title: One-parameter unitary groups and their generators
subtitle: G2 lecture 092000 · baseline companion · needs expansion
adaptation: First-pass source-derived outline. Section excerpts and any vector equation come from the spoken lecture and its display-only mathematics appendix. Expand with worked mathematics, proofs and topic-specific diagrams.

slides.title: The problem and its setting
slides.lead: In finite dimensions a self-adjoint matrix A produces a unitary motion by exponentiating imaginary t times A.
body: Every vector has a derivative, because A acts on every vector. For an unbounded self-adjoint operator, the unitary motion still acts on every vector, but the infinitesimal derivative exists only on a particular dense domain. That difference is the core of Stone's theorem and a major tool for unbounded perturbation theory. Strongly continuous unitary groups are determined by self-adjoint generators.

slides.title: The definition of a unitary group
slides.lead: A one-parameter unitary group is a family U of t, indexed by all real times, satisfying three properties.
body: Each U of t is a unitary operator, so it preserves inner products and has inverse equal to its adjoint. The group law says U of s plus t equals U of s followed by U of t. And U of zero is the identity. We also require strong continuity: for every fixed vector x, U of t x approaches x as t approaches zero. Because the operators are unitary, continuity at zero implies continuity at every time. The difference between U of t x and U of s x has the same length as the difference between U of t minus s applied to x and x.

slides.title: Building the group from a spectral measure
body: Its spectral theorem defines bounded functions of A. For each real t, the scalar function lambda mapped to the complex exponential of imaginary t times lambda has absolute value one. Therefore its spectral integral defines a bounded unitary operator U of t. We can call it the exponential of imaginary t A, provided we remember that this notation comes from functional calculus, not from an operator-norm power series in an unbounded A. The group law follows by multiplying the scalar spectral functions. The product of the exponentials at times s and t is the exponential at time s plus t. The value at time zero is one.

slides.title: The derivative selects the operator domain
slides.lead: Now take x in D of A.
body: We can divide the difference U of t x minus x by imaginary t. At a fixed spectral value lambda, the scalar quotient converges to lambda. Its magnitude is at most the absolute value of lambda, using the elementary inequality that the distance from the complex exponential of imaginary u to one is at most the absolute value of u. The domain condition for A is exactly the integrability of lambda squared against the spectral measure of x. Dominated convergence thus proves that the difference quotient converges in H to A x. So every vector in D of A admits the derivative, and its generator value is A x.

slides.title: A fast-rotation example
slides.lead: Return to ell two with A acting diagonally by N on the N-th coordinate.
body: The unitary group multiplies that coordinate by the complex exponential of imaginary t times N. For any fixed square-summable sequence x, the motion is strongly continuous. To check it without integrals, split x into its first finitely many coordinates and a tail. The finite part is continuous in t. The tail stays small, because each coordinate receives a phase of modulus one. But the group is not continuous in operator norm at zero. Set t equal to pi divided by N and test the N-th basis vector. Its phase is negative one, so the output is the negative of the original vector. Their distance is two.

slides.title: The generator and its sign
slides.lead: There are two common sign conventions.
body: One writes U of t as the exponential of imaginary t A. With that choice, the quotient of U of t x minus x by imaginary t converges to A x. Another convention writes U of t as the exponential of negative imaginary t A and inserts the opposite sign in the generator definition. Both are legitimate. We must keep the definition of the generator synchronized with the exponential used to construct the group. With the convention U of t equals the exponential of positive i times t A, the generator is recovered using division by i. Reversing the sign in the exponential reverses the corresponding generator convention.

slides.title: The converse direction of Stone's theorem
slides.lead: Suppose now that we start with an abstract strongly continuous unitary group, not with a self-adjoint operator.
body: We can define its infinitesimal generator using the vectors for which the appropriate difference quotient converges. One proves that this operator is symmetric by differentiating the inner-product preservation identity. The harder step is self-adjointness. Symmetry alone would not be sufficient. The group itself provides the missing resolvents. Consider an exponentially damped integral of U of t over positive times. Its norm is bounded by the integral of the damping exponential.

slides.title: Why the group helps with Sylvester equations
slides.lead: Unitary groups make it possible to compare two self-adjoint operators through bounded, everywhere-defined motions, even when the generators themselves are unbounded.
body: An expression such as U A of t, followed by a bounded operator C, followed by U B of negative t is always a bounded operator. We can integrate this expression against a suitable scalar kernel to build a candidate solution of a Sylvester equation. But when we differentiate such an expression to recover A X minus X B, the domains return.
